RULING BY THE CHAIRMAN 
On the issue of speech by Shri Ram Jethmalani 
in a matter on which he may have a pecuniary 
or other interest 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Members, on 24.8.2001. while participating in a 
discussion on the Calling Attention Motion on Disinvestment, Shri Ram 
Jethmalani, in the course of his speech, stated that he had a professional interest 
i n the matter under debate as he is the advisor to the Hindujas in the Bofors case. 
The propriety of his participation in such a discussion was raised by several 
Members, and the Vice-Chairman. Shri T. N. Chaturvedi, then stated that the 
matter would be referred to the Chairman for a ruling. 
In the meanwhile, on 27.8.2001, Shri Ram Jethmalani has also written a 
letter to me. with a copy to the Prime Minister, the Home Minister, Shri L. K. 
Advani, the Minister of Disinvestment, Shri Arun Shourie, Shri Kapil Sibal and 
Shri Fali S. Nariman, wherein he has stated that there is no prohibition in 
participation in such cases but only a duty to disclose the pecuniary or other 
interest. He has stated that he had no pecuniary interest in the Bofors case and 
that his interest in the discharge or acquittal in the criminal case has nothing to 
do with the Air India disinvestment process. 
I have considered the matter. While it is true that there is no rule, at 
present, which prohibits a Member of this House from speaking on a subject of 
public interest merely because it affects the case of a person who is the Member's 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
client in that or another matter, the question is ultimately one of propriety, and I think, the 
House will agree with me that this has to be left to the good sense of the Member 
concerned. 
In this connection. I also refer to a similar issue which came up in this House 
during a Short Duration Discussion on 30.12.1993 on the JPC Report on Banking 
Transactions, when a Member — in fact , Shri Ram Jethmalani, — disclosed his 
interest in the matter under discussion and I quote: "Sir, this scam happens to be 
connected with somebody with whom I am professionally associated. All textbooks 
on parliamentary practice require that when a Member of the House has some interest 
other than his being a Member of this House, it is his duly to disclose it. I am formally 
disclosing it, though the whole of the House is aware that 1 am professionally interested 
in Mr. Harshad Mehta. But I am formally declaring it so that it should not be said that I 
did not perform my duty under the rule of parliamentary ethics." Further, he had said 
and I quote: "Sir. 1 propose to carry this rule of parliamentary ethics a little further. I 
will subject myself to a voluntary restraint of not commenting on that portion of the 
controversy which has anything to do with Mr. Harshad Mehta, or, his controversy 
with the Prime Minister, or, about Rs. 1 crore payment. Nobody need worry because the 
Parliamentary Committee refused to go into this issue and said that this matter requires 
to be investigated later on. I will not go into this controversy. In fact. I will not refer to 
any transactions of Mr. Harshad Mehta." 
This was accepted as a reasonable practice in the absence of any rules in the 
House. 
Hon. Members are aware that this House had adopted on 15.12.1999, the Second 
Report of the Ethics Committee, Para 6 of which reads as follows: "There arc occasions 
when a Member may have direct, indirect or specific pecuniary interest in a matter 
being considered by the House or a Committee thereof. In such a case, he may declare 
the nature of such interest, notwithstanding any registration of his interests in the 
Register, and desist from participating in any such debate or vote taking place in the 
House or its Committees, before making such declaration." 
Until rules of procedure relating to ethical conduct are framed, I think, it would 
be appropriate for Members to continue to follow this practice of declaring their pecuniary 
or other interest at the very outset of their speech. 
With this, the matter may be treated as closed.

Literacy Drive 
562. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: † 
           DR. KARAN SINGH:  
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state whether the programmes like Operation Black Board and Adult Literacy 
Campaign, implemented to give a special thrust to literacy drive, have been 
given a go by: if not. the details of the schemes being implemented in pursuance 
of the literacy drive under the Ninth Five Year Plan, the expenditure incurred 
thereon, so far. and the targets fixed and achieved so far? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT: (DR MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Regarding Literacy Drive 
Government of India has adopted a two-pronged approach to improve 
literacy in the country. 
* Universalisation of Elementary Education through enrolment of all 
children in 6-14 year age group and reducing drop-out rates. 
* Providing functional literacy to non-literates in 15-35 year age group. 
List of schemes to support these goals is at Statement I {see below) 
This includes Operation Black Board, in which estimated expenditure in 
lXth Plan will be Rs. 1773.3 crore, a step up of about 60% over the VIII* Plan 
period expenditure of Rs. 1108.7 crore. 
The Adult literacy programmes have however been restructured to meet 
the changing requirement of the sector with the introduction of Continuing 
Education Scheme during the IXth Five Year Plan. 
Government has placed a lot of empha sis in the sector of elementary 
education to give a push to total literacy in the country.

In pursuance of the literacy drive a new scheme of Sana Shiksha Abhiyan 
has also been recently approved by th e Government. This has a holistic and 
convergent approach to implement Universalisation of Elementary Education in 
a mission mode with a clear district focus. The goals of Sana Shiksha Abhiyan 
are as follows:— 
• All the children in school Education Guarantee scheme Centre. 
Alternate school. 'Back-to-schooL Camp by 2003. 
• All children complete five year primary education by 2007. 
• All children complete eight years of schooling by 2010. 
• Focus on Elementary Education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
• Bridge all gender and social gaps at primary stage by 2007 and 
Elementary Education level by 2010. 
• Universal retention by 2010. 
Census 2001 (Provisional) has indicated that India has made significant 
progress in the field of literacy during the last decade. The salient points of the 
census report on literacy are: 
• Literacy rate is 65.38 percent today as against 52.21 percent in 1991. 
• The 13.17 percentage points increase in literacy rate is the highest in any 
decade.

percentage points in 1991 to 21.7 percentage points in 2001. 
National Literacy Mission had receive d the prestigious Noma Literacy 
Award in 1999 for outstanding efforts in spreading literacy, creating awareness

Statement 
Formulation of Decisions on Education 
NATIONAL CURRICULUM FRAMEWORK FOR SCHOOL EDUCATION 
The Process of Development and Consultation 
The process of curriculum renewal for school education began in NCERT 
in 1996-97. In 1999 an internal curriculum group was constituted to expedite the 
process. The curriculum group visited all the departments and constituent units 
of NCERT located in Delhi and at Ajmer. Bhopal. Bhubaneswar and Mysore. It 
held intensive consultations with academ ics including school teachers. It also 
invited ten eminent scientists and educationists for interaction on the emerging 
curriculum issues in school education. This process resulted in development of 
a Discussion Document which was released in January 2000 and made available 
to all the State Ministers of School Education (Primary. Secondary and Senior 
Secondary), Education Secretaries and heads of all State level institutions 
connected with school education. In addition it was also made available to 
institutions, organisations. NGOs, universities, newspaper editors, experts and 
eminent educationists. It was put on the NCERT website and a copy was available 
to anybody who requested for it in view of its wide coverage in the press and 
media. The Discussion Document was made available to even faculty member

of NCERT in Delhi and its constituent Units. They were requested to give their 
written co mmments as well. 
Based upon these consultations and inputs received from various sources, 
the curriculum group developed the Curriculum Framework for School Education 
and it was released on November 14.2000 by the Minister for Human Resource 
Development. This was made available to all the state functionaries by NCERT. 
The Hon'ble Minister for Human Resource Development addressed letters to 
Chief Ministers of Slates. Union Ministers, State Ministers and political leaders 
of various parties enclosing a copy of the document and requesting them to get 
it examined and for implementing it in a desirable manner. Education Secretary 
has written to the States/UTs Education Secretaries for a report on the 
implementation of the Curriculum Framework 
The Document was specifically discus s in the Annual Conferences of 
School Education Secretaries held in April. 2001, where the Director. NCERT 
made a detailed presentation, it was also discussed in the General Body meeting 
of the NCERT held on 13th December 2000 where the Education Ministers of the 
States/UTs are members.

Discrimination against the farmers in WTO Agreement 
*568 SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO : Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the WTO agreement is very discriminatory against the farmers 
of developing countries, as it is against the farmers of developed countries; 
?2 

[31 August 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) what is the limit of subsidy on farm products in developing countries 
and what is the limit on such products in developed countries; and 
(c) the reasons for this discrimination and whether this question would be 
taken up with the WTO ? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) WTO 
Agreement provides a non discriminatory, rule based, predictable multilateral 
framework for trade among member co untries. Under the Agreement on 
Agriculture, the permissible level (de-minimis) of domestic support expressed in 
terms of Aggregate Measure of Support (Amber Box) is 10% and 5% of the total 
value of the agricultural produce respectively for developing countries and 
developed countries. The domestic support given to low income or resource 
poor farmers in developing countries is also excluded from the Aggregate Measure 
of Support. 
During the on-going agricultural negotiations under Article 20 of the 
Agreement on Agriculture, India has demanded additional flexibility for 
developing countries in providing subsidies or domestic support to take care of 
their food security, poverty alleviation and rural employment concerns.

THEMIMSTEROFHUMANRESOURCEDEVELOPMENT(DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The goal of the National Policy for the Empowerment of Women is to 
bring about the advancement, development and empowerment of women. 
Specifically, the objectives of this Policy include : 
(i) Creating an environment through positive economic and social 
policies for full development of women to enable them to realize 
their full potential; 
33

(ii) The de-jure and de-facto enjoyment of all human rights and 
fundamental freedom by women on equal basis with men in all 
spheres—political, economic, social, cultural and civil; 
(iii) Equal access to participation and decision making of women in social, 
political and economic life of the nation; 
(iv) Equal access to women to health care, quality education at all levels, 
career and vocational guidance, employment, equal remuneration, 
occupational health and safety, social security and public office 
etc.; 
(v) Strengthening legal systems aime d at elimination of all forms of 
discrimination agains women; 
(vi) Changing societal attitudes and community practices by active 
participation and involvement of both men and women; 
(vii) Mainstreaming a gender perspective in the development process; 
(viii) Elimination of discrimination and all forms of violence against women 
and the girl child; and 
fix) Building and strengthening partnerships with civil society, 
particularly women's organizations. 
The National Policy for the Empowerment of Women has been widely 
disseminated to Central Ministries/Departments, State Governments, Non-

Indo-US Science and Technology Forum 
*573. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India and US have signed an agreement to set 
up an Indo-US Science and Technology Forum; 
38 

[31 August, 2001] RAJ YA SABHA 
(b) if so. the main objectives of the Forum; and 
(c) how the Government plan to implement these objectives ? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) An Agreement to establish the Indo-US Science 
and Technology Forum was concluded on March 21. 2000. 
The aim of the Forum is to facilitate and promote the interaction in India 
and the United States of government, academia and industry in science and 
technology and other related areas. The main objectives of the Forum are : 
• to focus on issues of common concern and activities of mutual 
benefit, while exploring trends in S & T 
• to create a comprehensive electronic reference source for Indo-US 
S&T cooperation 
• to promote electronic exchange and dissemination of information 
and opportunities in bilateral S&T cooperation 
• to commission studies, reports and papers and promote Indo-US 
cooperation in R&D and transfer of technology 
• to facilitate and promote joint collaborative projects and programmes 
and organize workshops, seminars, symposia, courses and training 
programmes 
• to establish-Indo-US Centres for excellence at places in India. 
To ensure that objectives of the Forum conform to highest standards of 
excellence, a Governing Body of eminent persons has been established with 
equal (seven members each) Indian and US representation. The Governing Body 
consists of highly respected representatives from government, industry, academia 
and private organizations. It provides guidance and leadership by monitoring 
present activities and trends in bilatera l science and technology cooperation 
and makes recommendations and identifies priorities and directions for future 
cooperation. The Governing Body is empowered to constitute advisory groups 
or committees for specific purposes as required.

STATEMENT 
Trade of Animal Skins in Delhi 
(1) Steps taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting 
and commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have been set 
up in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(2) Steps taken at National level: 
(0 Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Offices 
for wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the 
country to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute 
wildlife offenders. Ami poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(iii) Financial and technical help is being extended to the States under 
various Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project 
Elephant, Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-
development around Protected Areas for enhancing the capacity 
and infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to 
wild animals. Financial assistance is, in particular, being provided 
for raising 'Strike Forces' and providing arms to the protection staff 
for combating the organised poachers. Assistance is also provided 
for giving rewards to the informers for eliciting information about 
poachers and smugglers. 
(iv) A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set 
up under the chairmanship of Secr etary, Environment & Forests, 
Government of India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife

(v) Export of wild animals and their derivatives is prohibited under EXIM policy. 
(vi) A National Conference of Forests and Environment Ministers of State 
Government was held on 29th and 30th January, 2001. It was resolved to 
organise existing protection staff into viable formations for effective 
control of poaching and to create enforcement infrastructure both 
within and out side protected areas. 
(vii) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and illegal trade 
in wildlife. 
(3) Steps taken at International level. 
(i) Government of India seeks international Co-operation under the 
provisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species 
of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade in wildlife 
items. 
(ii) To control transboundary trade a protocol has been signed with Peoples'

STATEMENT-I 
Gist of major recommendations contained in the Report of the National 
Expert Committee on Women Prisoners headed by Justice Krishna Iyer 
1. Policy Making and Monitoring 
(a) A National Policy on Custodial Justice to women should be formulated 
and adopted. A draft policy was suggested by the Expert Committee 
(b) National Authority on Custodial Justice to Women (NACJW) should 
be constituted to overview and monitor the implementation of the National 
Policy. 
(c) One Member of NACJW be designated as the Ombudsman for Custodial 
Institution for Women in India. 
2. Judicial 
(a) State level ACJAW and Ombudsman be also set up. 
(i) Depending on the individual preferences of States, either the jurisdiction 
of Family Court constituted under the Family Court Act 1984 be extended or the 
Women's Court should be instituted to dispense justice to women. But it should 
be mandatory for the states to create a separate and specialized justice dispensing 
modality to women. 
(b) Nari Bandigriha Adalat in the na ture of mobile judicial camps for 
rendering speedy redress to women in custody. 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
3. Legislative 
(a) Article 252 of the Constitution of India should be invoked to get the / 
concurrence of two or more States to bring uniform Comprehensive Prison and Prisoner 
Act throughout the country. 
(b) A comprehensive code to cover the administration of all custodial 
institutions should also be formulated. 
(c) Critical assessment of the efficacy and relevance of various legislations bearing 
on women's siatus in custody and their criminality'should be undertaken by the Law 
Commission. 
(d) Appropriate amendment should be made in the IPC, CrPC, Prison Act, 1894 
and Police Act 1861 to reflect the special needs of women in custody. 
(e) The new Mental Health Bill should reflect the specific recommendations of the 
Committee in lespect of the custody and treatment of non-criminal and criminal 
lunatic women. 
4. Administrative 
A. Prisons 
(a) A cadre of prison service should be set up. 
(b) There should be enhanced and protected representation of women in the 
prison cadre. 
(c) There should be women DIG at the State HQ preferably from prison service 
to look after the work relating to women prisons. 
(d) Women Superintendents of Women prisons should be made fully 
autonomous. 
(e) There should be permanent wardens and matrons., 
(0 Prisoner's Council should be set up in every prison. 
(g) Socio-legal counseling cells should be set up in every prison (h) 
Released Prisoner's Aid Societies should operate in every district.

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Prison amenities for women and their children should be clearly identified 
preferably in a separate volume of the Prison Manual. 
B. Police 
(a) A cadre of Women Police should be set up. 
(b) It should oe mandatory for each Police Station to have separate lock up 
for women prisoners. 
(c) A model Police Manual should be compiled and this should earn 
indicative standards of minimum space and other facilities and procedures 
applicable to women when in Police custody. 
(d) Women's Assistance Police Unit should be created. 
C. Social Welfare and Mental Health Custodial Institutions

should be devised.

(e) Socio-legal counselling cells should operate in these institutes. 
(f) Inmates Councils should be set up in these institutions. 
(g) An escort corps with necessary police powers should be developed to 
provide escorting services to these institutions. 
5. Participative Structure

institutions alongwith full right! ^pect institutional records and interview

Pension Liabilities of the Railways 
4392. SHRI RS. GAVAI: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Railways have received the Rakesh Mohan Committee 
report on its pension liabilities; 
(b) if so, the details of recommendations made by the Committee; and 
(c) the reaction of the Railways thereto ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) Relevant extracts of the Report on Pension Liabilities are enclosed as 
Statement (See below). 
(c) The Report is under examination. 
Statement 
Railways Pension Fund 
The Railways established the Railway Pension Fund in 1964. The 
underlying intentions of the creators of this fund were good : 
*it was to be funded out of railway revenues; 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
*it would meet current payments to railway pensioners; 
*it would build up a fund to meet liabilities for future pension benefits; 
*it would be financed on the basis of independent actuarial calculations such 
that it would have a sufficient balance to meet its liabilities. 
The reality has been quite different in the absence of an actuarial assessment 
and faced with competing demands for funds, IR has been unable to build up a funded 
scheme. Even today, IR is only managing to pay into the fund what the fund has to pay 
out to meet its current liabilities; even though some balances were accumulated in the 
Fund, .they have been almost completely depleted to meet the commitments made on 
the basis of the Fifth Central Pay Commission (FCPC). 
To summarise, the Railways Pension Funds has no funds available to meet its 
liabilities. The questions thus arise how should that liability be considered and how can it 
be met ? 
Railway Staff Strength and Pensioners Today 
Indian Railways today has approximtely 1.5 million serving employees and 
almost 1.1 milllion pensioners. While the Railways staff strength has remained constant 
around 1.5—1.6 million since 1975, the number of pensioners has been increasing 
consistently over the same period'—from 100,000 in 1975 to 700,000 in 1990 and 
approximately 1.1 million today. 
Railway Pensioners in the Future 
One can look at a pensions liability as being a cost which the Current 
employees have to bear (or, better, as a cost which has to be met by revenue earned by 
those current employees). This allows one to consider two interesting statistics; the 
pensioners per current employee ratio and the total pension cost as proportion of total 
operating cost. This does not mean that the Expert Group believes that this is a problem 
which should be borne by the current employees— far from it. Rather, these statistics are 
useful to understand the nature of the problem facing Railways and its owner.

Focusing on the issues 
What do all of these numbers tell us ? The view of the Expert Group is that they 
indicate the scale of the problem—but, as noted above, they do not help in suggesting a 
solution. We, therefore, turn to the next question—why can't Railways just continue 
to bear these costs on the same basis ? 
It could—in much the same way as it is going to have to bear the various other 
costs associated with running a railway business—like the third party debt it inherits, 
wages, capital expenditure etc.—i.e. IR could treat the pension liability as just 
another debt. 
However, the Expert Group questions whether that is the right approach for a 
number of reasons: 
* 'Pay-as-you-go' systems such as th at in place in IR are universally 
acknowledged to be highly flawed. They fail the fundamental principle of 
prudence which all business should adopt (accruing funds to meet future 
liabilities as these liabilities accrue), they provide no security to employees, 
they hinder employee choice and they are particularly dangerous in business 
where efficiencies are improving dramatically. In essence, such system are 
not sustainable in commercial concerns: 
* At a practical level, and a discussed in section 5.8 railways is utterly reliant 
on Gol to meet operating and capital shortfalls i.e. IR can not serve its 
liabilities anyway. So there is no point in just 'leaving' the liability with IR-it 
will come straight back to Gol anyway, 
* One of the key objectives of the Expert Group is to recommend a structure 
which going forward allows IR to be run as a going concern on commercial 
terms. Saddling it with a vast liability built up over the past 60 or 70 years 
imposes an unnecessary burden which its competitors in India and its 
comparators and peers around the world do not have to carry; and 
* The employees of IR are entitled to some measure of security as to their 
pension benefits- with IR emerging into a riskier world, it may be preferable to 
insulate those benefits from the business. 
Is There a solution? 
Yes—in fact there are many. This is  an issue which has been faced by 
numerous businesses all over the world. It has been seen most frequently in 
156 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
government owned businesses (which, traditionally, treat business employees 
like civil servants and pay pensions on a PAYG basis out of the exchequer) as 
they move towards more commercial structures (and, in many cases, towards 
partial or complete private sector ownership). 
So, how should IR deal with this ? Step 1 is to assess the problem. This 
is most easily done if one can separatre the liabilities into three categories : 
A. Liabilities to past employees; 
B. Future liabilities to current employees in respect of their pensions 
entitlements accrued for past service; and 
C. Liabilities which will accrue in the future to employees (current and 
future) in respect of future employment. 
Category C liabilities are the easiest to  deal with- these are—'normal' 
costs of employment which any employer bears and which should therefore be 
allocated to IR (albeit that Gol may be paying or contributing to them for a few 
years via its subsidy). 
Category A and B liabilities are rather different. These are liabilities which 
have already been run up-but for which no cash fund is available. These liabilities 
have been estimated as at April 30,2000 at about Rs 40.000 crore. This does not 
mean that Rs 40,000 crore is needed immediately—rather that this is the cash 
sum which, if invested today, would be sufficient (using its opening corpus and 
future investment income) to meet those accrued liabilities as they fall due. 
How can such a fund be built up? that is a political question. The Expert 
Group's recommendation is that it be built up over a relatively short period (say 
in five years) by contributions from Gol either direct or via Railways. A final 
question needs to be answered - what form should such a fund take ? 
As mentioned above, there are numerous precedents. Our recommendation 
is as follows: 
1. Gol and IR should aim to create a fully-funded scheme; 
2. The fund should be independent of IR with an independent board 
of trustees and a clear set of rules governing, inter alia, investment 
principles and employee entitlements; 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
3. IR should pay contributions into the fund on an on-going basis to build 
up the corpus to meet Category C liabilities. It may be worthwhile 
(given point (8) below) to treat these liabilities differently—in that 
employees' benefits derived from future employment could be tied to 
actual performance of the invested funds rather than to the existing 
index-linked basis; 
4. The sum required to meet the Category A and B liabilities should be 
contributed by Gol (ideally directly rather than via Railways) over a 
limited period (say five years) from the exchequer/general reserve; 
5. The fund should be sufficiently flexible to allow changes (particularly to allow 
transfer of pension rights) as the pension industry matures in India; 
6. Gol should take over this liability from IR as part of the restructring and 
corporatisation process (a normal route being for Gol to receive equity to 
the same value); 
7. Gol and IR should ensure that employees and pensioners understand the 
changes and understand their impact on each of them; 
8. It may be sensible for Gol and IR to ensure that Category A and B 
benefits available under the new scheme cannot fall below those which 
would have been available under the old scheme.

*541. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
SHRI P.PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the major findings of the latest Human Development Report released some 
time back by the United Nations, regarding growth and development achieved by 
various countries; 
(b) the position assigned to India in realising higher standards of life and greater 
human welfare; and 
(c) the measures to be adopted to take care of the sectors where India has lagged 
behind? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE): (a) to (c) The Human Development Report (HDR) 2001, released recently 
by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) indicates that in most 
countries of the world, indices of Human Development have been improving over the 
past twenty five years. However, in some twenty countries in Africa, Eastern Europe and 
the former Soviet Union, they have been deteriorating. 
This year's Report assesses the progress made by countries towards targets set 
in the UN Millennium Declaration goals for poverty eradication. Just 11 developing 
countries, including India are on track to meet the goal of having poverty by 2015, but 70 
countries are far beh od or slipping. 
The Report is dedicated to the theme "Making New Technologies Work for 
Human Development". It terms technology as a tool for development and notes with 
concern the disparities in the spread of technology both between 
*The sitting of the Rajya Sabha on Thursday, the 30th August, 2001

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
and within countries. The Report ranks countries by the level of diffusion of 
technology in each country as per a Technology Achievement Index (TAI). The 
Report recognises India as home to a world class technology hub in Bangalore 
and classifies it among dynamic adopters. 
India's rank in the Human Development Index (HDI) is 115 among 162 
countries and territories ranked by the UNDP's HDR for 2001. The ranks of our 
South Asian neighbours on the HDI are: Bangladesh -132, Bhutan -130. Maldives 
- 77, Nepal -129. Pakistan • 127 and Sri Lanka -81. 
India has also improved its Human Poverty Index (HPI) rank from 58 out of 
85 countries in HDR 2000 to 55 out of 90 in HDR 2001. The ranks of some of our 
South Asian neighbours in HPI are Bangladesh - 73. Maldives - 25. Nepal - 77. 
Pakistan - 65 and Sri Lanka-31. 
India's HDI value has improved from 0.406 in 1975 to 0.510 in 1990 and 
0.571 in 1999. The bulk of the improvement in the HDI in the 1990s has been due 
to the improvements in the income component of the index. Social development 
indicators did also improve during the last few years but their rate of improvement 
has not kept pace with that of GDP per capita expressed in terms of Purchasing 
Power Parity. This is especially true of life expectancy, infant mortality rate, adult 
literacy and the combined enrolment ratio. 
The Social sector has received greater thrust in the last few years, especially 
elementary education and family welfare. They will also continue to be among 
the priority sectors during the Tenth Five Year Plan.

a judgement delivered on 22.09.2000 in the matter of T.N. Godavarman 
Thirumulkpad Vs. Union of India and Santosh Bharti Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while deciding the question as to who is the authority 
competent to write Confidential Report of an officer belonging to the Indian 
Forest Service (IFS) within the meaning of the provisions of All India Service 
(Confidential Rolls) Rules, 1970, had held that upto the officer of the rank of 
Additional Principal Chief Conservator of Forests, the reporting authority has to 
be the immediately superior officer within the Forest Department. The Supreme 
Court had taken note of the decision in State of Haryana Vs. Shri P. C. Wadhwa 
and Anr. 1987 (2) SCR. 1030 and directed the State of Madhya Pradesh to pass 
appropriate orders enu lerating the reporting authorities. 
 
Following the judgement in PC. Wadhwa case, referred to above, the All 
India Service (Confidential Rolls) Rules, 1970 had been amended on 8.12.87. Rule 
2(a), 2(e) and 2(f) of these Rules defining 'accepting authority', 'reporting

authority1 and 'reviewing authority' respectively were amended to provide that 
such authority should be one supervising the performance of the officer and an 
explanation was also added providing that the authority or authorities supervising 
the performance of the officer shall not necessarily mean an authority or authorities 
belonging to the same service to which the reporting or the reviewing authority, 
as the case maj be, belongs. 
 
Looking to the above Rule position as amended in 1987 and considering the 
implications of the judgement on inter-departmental coordination at the field 
level, the Ministry of Environment & Forests as the Cadre Controlling Authority 
for the Indian Forest Service, has been advised to file a review petition in the 
Supreme Court.

Authorities for Indian Police Service (IPS) and the Indian Forest Service (IFS)

Associations in this regard.

trafficking in the region emanating from Afghanistan were discussed;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI 
OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) India and Russia had decided to set up a Joint Working Group 
on Afghanistan during the visit of His Excellency Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the 
Russian Federation to India on October 2-5, 2000. The first meeting of the group was 
held in New Delhi on November 20-21,2000. The Russian delegation was led by H.E. 
Mr. V. Trubnikov, First Deputy Foreign Minister of the Russian Federation. During this 
meeting both sides reviewed the situation prevailing in Afghanistan in all its 
dimensions. 
(b) and (c) India and Russia noted th at the Taliban controlled areas of 
Afghanistan had become centres for training, promotion and shelter of 
international terrorists. The two sides also recognised that the Taliban controlled 
areas of Afghanistan had become the largest producers of opium in the world. They 
called upon the Taliban to stop the illegal production of opium. Both sides agreed to 
continue their cooperation at the bilateral level as well multilaterally to address the 
threat of terrorism and illegal narcotics emanating from Afghanistan. 
267 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
(d) During the last meeting of the Indo-Russian Joint Working Group on 
Afghanistan, which was held in Moscow on June 25-26, 2001, in-depth discussions 
were held on the issues pertaining to the situation in Afghanistan and around it These 
included issues of Taliban held areas in Afghanistan having become nerve centres and 
breeding ground for terrorists and separatist forces, narcotics and extremist ideologies; 
the need for effective implementation of UN Security Council Resolutions No. 1267 
and No. 1333 and end of foreign interference in Afghan Affairs; unacceptability of 
discriminatory policies of the Taliban in particular the recent Taliban decree, 
prescribing distinctive dress code and wearing of distinguishing marks for Afghan 
Hindus and Sikhs, and importance of coordinated international cooperation for 
reducing the fall out and eventually for the elimination of negative forces of terrorism, 
narcotics and extremist ideologies emanating from the Taliban held areas in Afghanistan. 
The two sides agreed to continue close cooperation at the bilateral level as well as 
multilaterally to address the threats of terrorist forces, narco-terrorism and extremist

Illegal foreign occupation in Indian Territory 
4183. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
SARDAR GURCHARAN SINGH TOHRA:

(a) the details of the Indian territory/land under illegal occupation of

272 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) since when such lands are under foreign occupation; and 
(c) the efforts made last by Government of India to reclaim the territory in 
each case ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) 
Pakistan 
Pakistan has forcibly and illegally occupied approximately 78,000 sq. kms. 
of Indian territory in the State of Jammu & Kashmir. Under the Simla Agreement 
and the Lahore Declaration, which are the cornerstones of our bilateral relations. 
Government are committed to resolving all issues with Pakistan peacefully 
through bilateral discussions. 
China 
China illegally occupies approximately 38,000 sq. kms. of Indian territory 
in the State of Jammu & Kashmir. In addition, under the so-called Sino-Pakistan 
Boundary Agreement of 1963, Pakistan illegally ceded 5,180. sq. kms. of Indian 
territory in Pakistan occupied Kashmir to China. India and China are seeking a 
fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement of the boundary question 
through peaceful consultations. 
Bangladesh 
Along the International Boundary between the two countries, Bangladesh 
is estimated to have an area of 2,749 acres adversely possessed and India an 
area of 29,228 acres. These are areas possessed by nationals of the other country 
than the one to which the land belongs. 
The 1974 Agreement between the Government of the Republic of India 
and the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh concerning the 
demarcation of the land boundary between India and Bangladesh and related 
matters, provides for exchange of adverse possessions. 
The first meeting of the India—Bangladesh Joint Boundary Working 
Groups on Border Demarcation, and on Enclaves and Adversely Possessed 
Territories was held in Dhaka from July 2-4,2001. Pending implementation of 
the Land Boundary Agreement by mutu al agreement, both sides reiterated 
their commitment to maintaining status quo and peace and tranquility on the 
border.

Statement 
Incentives to IT Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been rationalised 
and extended uniformly to all sectors without any threshold limit on 
payment of 5% duty. 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to the 
Information Technology sector, with the exception of Business-to-
consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Power of approvals of the designated officers of MIT for 
implementation of STP and EHTP Schemes have been further 
enhanced upto US $ 20 million. 
4. Accelerated depreciation norms for computers and computer 
peripherals for electronic units under Export Oriented schemes (EOU/ 
EPZ/STP/EHTP) have been enhanced. These shall stand depreciated 
to overall limit of 90% over a period of 3 years instead of around 
5 years earlier. The depreciation on computers has been allowed 
@60%. 
5. DTA access upto 50% of the FOB value of export is permitted for 
electronics hardware units under EOU/EP27EHTP schemes and the 
software units under EOU/EPZ/STP schemes. Broadbanding is 
permitted in the DTA sales of Hardware units for items covered in 
the Letter of Permission. 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001] 
6. Special Economic Zones are being set up to enable hassle free 
manufacturing and trading for export purposes. 
7. Value addition norms for Rupee exports to Russia reduced from 
100% to 33% under Advance Licensing Scheme. 
8. In the Budget 2001-02, the peak  rate of customs duty continues 
@35%. Customs duty surcharge @ 10% has been abolished on all 
imports, in general but Special Additional Duty (SAD) @ 4% 
continues on all imports, except specific exemptions. In the 2000-01 
Budget, Customs duty on Computers and Peripherals had been 
reduced from 20% to 15% and continues to be same. The Customs 
duty on all storage devices, integrated circuits, microprocessors, 
data display tubes and deflection components of color monitors 
also continues at 0%. In the 2001-02 Budget, Customs duty on 
Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items of WTO (IT and 
. Telecom products) has been reduced from existing 20-25% to 15%. 
The concessional rate of customs duty for specified raw materials 
for the electronics industry continues. 
9. In the Budget 2001 -02, the Central Excise duty structure has been 
rationalised from multiple rates to single rate of 16% and single rate 
of Special Excise Duty (SED) @ 16%. 
10. Information Technology Software is exempted from Customs and 
Excise Duty. 
11. EOU/EPZ/STP/EHTP units are exempted from payment of Income 
Tax on export profits, upto 2010, in terms of Sections 10A and 10B of 
the Income Tax Act. 
12. Definition of Computer Software, as in Section 80 HHE of the Income 
Tax Act has been widened to include transmission of data. 
13. Benefit of Section 80 HHE is available to supporting software 
developers. 
14. Exemption of withholding tax on interest on External Commercial 
Borrowings (ECBs) has been extended to the IT sector. 
15. Income by way of dividends or long-term capital gains of a \fenture 
Capital Fund or \fenture Capital company from investment made by 
294 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
way of equity shares in a Venture Capital Undertaking, which has been 
expanded to include the Software and IT sectors, will henceforth not be 
included in computing the total income. 
16. To give thrust to Venture Capital finance, SEBI has been made the single 
point nodal agency for registration and regulation of both domestic and 
overseas venture capital funds. 
17. There will be no tax on distributed or undistributed income of \fenture Capital 
Funds. The income distributed by the VCFs will only be taxed in the 
hands of the investors at the rates applicable to the nature of the income. 
VCFs will continue to be eligible for exemption even if the shares of the VC 
undertaking in which the VCFs have made the initial investment are 
subsequently listed in a recognised stock exchange in India. 
18. Under policy on portfolio investment, Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls) are 
permitted to invest in a company upto an aggregate of 24% of equity shares, 
extendable upto 40% subject to approvals. This limit has been raised from 
40% to 49% in the Budget 2001-02. 
19. Under the Employee Stock Option Scheme, income tax payable on income 
from GDRs purchased in foreign currency by a resident employee of IT 
software and service companies, shall be at a concessional rate of 
10%. 
20. Tax holiday under provisions of Section 80-IA (Infrastructure Status) has 
been extended to Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and Broadband 
Network providers. 
21. Two-way fungibility has been permitted for ADRs/GDRs. Local shares 
can now be reconverted into ADRs/GDRs, subject to sectoral caps. 
22. To induce more investment for R&D activities, a weighted deduction of 125% 
on the sums paid to any university, college or an institution or a Scientific 
Research Association for the purposes of scientific, social or statistical 
research has been provided. 
23. Information Technology Act 2000 has been enacted. This act deals with 
Cyber Security, Cyber Crime and other information security related legal 
aspects. This will encourage expansion of e-commerce through internet.

4222. SHRI R. S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state :

4236. SHRI PARMESHWARKUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the PRIME

captioned "SC says forfeit corrupt officers property" appearing in the Times of 
India dated the 18th May, 2001; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSON NEL 
AND TRAINING OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES 
AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) In the news-
item, the Supreme Court has observed that several punishments, including 
forfeiture of property, were provided under Section 61 and 62 of the Indian Penal 
Code (IPC). However, these Sections were deleted by Indian Penal Code 
(Amendment) Act, 1921. The Apex Court has felt the need to re-introduce these 
provisions so as to have a deterrent effect on those bent upon accumulating 
wealth by misusing their post of power. 
(c) Though the provisions of this Sections have been repealed in 1921, the 
Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance 38 of 1944 provides for attachment of 
properties of the public servant who is accused of corruption. This can be done 
at the stage of trial of the concerned public servant thus ensuring mat during the 
pendency of the case, the concerned property is not disposed of. However, 
confiscation or forfeiture can take place only when the public servant has been 
convicted of corruption and amassing assets disproportionate to his known 
sources of income.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) The Planning Commission has prepared the 
Mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan (1997—2002) which contains a 
review of various Poverty Alleviation Programmes. The highlights of the Mid-

(d) The strategy for Poverty Alleviation includes acceleration of economic 
growth with a focus on employment intensive sectors, access to basic minimum 
services for improving the quality of life of the people and direct State intervention 
in the form of targeted anti poverty programmes. Anti-poverty programmes 
supplement the growth effort and prot ect the poor from destitution, sharp 
fluctuations in employment and incomes, and social insecurity. The specifically 
designed anti poverty programmes for generation of both self employment and 
wage employment in rural, areas have been redesigned and restructured in 
1999-2000 in order to enhance their efficacy/impact on the poor and improve 
their sustainability. Self and wage employment schemes in the urban areas were 
also restructured w.e.f. 01.12.1997 under Swarnjayanti Shahri Rozgar Yojana. The 
review of the restructured programmes would form part of the Tenth Plan exercise 
which has already started. 
STATEMENT 
High lights of Mid-Term Appraisal of the 
Ninth Five Year Plan (1997—2002) 
Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation Programmes 
Poverty-Alleviation Programmes 
Poverty had declined substantially in 1980s. Proportion of people below 
poverty line declined from 54.9 % in 1973-74 to 36 % in 1993-94. However, recent 
estimates suggest that the projections on reduction of proportion and number 
of people below poverty line made in the Ninth Plan have not been realised in the 
first two years of the plan period. 
340 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
This may be due to: sluggish agricultural growth which was also less well 
spread out; labour absorption did not increase hence slow down in growtli of 
real wages; failure of poverty alleviation and watershed development schemes; 
continuance of certain policies that act against the interest of the poorest, 
especially tribals; inadequate reach of TPDS to the poorest in the Northern and 
Eastern States; fiscal crisis caused by the Vth Pay Commission that led to 
reduced ability of the States to spend on social sectors; limited growtli of mral 
non-farm sector and poor governance. 
Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) evaluation points: sub-
critical investment; unviable projects; illiterate and unskilled beneficiaries with 
no experience in managing an enterprise; indifferent delivery of credit by banks, 
overcrowding of lending in certain projects such as dairy; under emphasis on 
activities like trading, service and even simple processing, poor targeting and 
selection of non-poor; rising indebtedness; scale of IRDP outstripped capacity 
of government and banks to absorb. 
Integrated Rural Development Programme-Allied Programmes: TRYSEM not 
dovetailed with IRDP. Non-existent training centres, nonpayment of stipend 
(Chhapra study). DWCRA did well in some States (A.P., Kerala, Gujarat). 
Sawarn Jayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (the successor to IRDP): aims at 
micro-enterprises with emphasis on cluster approach. It is a credit-cum-subsidy 
programme. Focus on self-help groups. In the past, subsidy orientation leads to 
corruption and distortion of objectives. Too early to evaluate. 
Jawahar Rozgar Yojana evaluation points: inadequate employment (11 
days as per concurrent evaluation); thin spread of resources; violation of material-
labour norms; corruption (fudging of muster rolls). Projects were executed by 
contractors who sometimes hired outside labourers at lower wages. Positive 
aspects: durable community assets an d empowerment of gram Panchayats. 
Redesigned in April 1999 as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana. Primary aim now 
rural infrastructure. Employment is secondary. Too early to evaluate. 
Employment Assurance Scheme, initially demand-driven. Funds went to 
better-off states. Evaluation by PEO: scheme is being executed through 
contractors in most of the States in violation of the central guidelines; me norm 
of 60:40 for wage and material is not maintained; the genuine muster ro! Is are not 
being maintained by the Gram Panchayats. Family cards have not been issued. 
ston of registration of job seekers with Gram Panchayats 
34! 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Central norms of earmarking, 40 per cent of funds for watershed development 
and 20 per cent for minor irrigation, have not been followed. 
From April 1999 restructured as the single wage employment scheme; 
became allocative; 30% of funds allocated to district reserved for areas suffering 
from endemic labour exodus/areas of distress. Need to shift focus only to backward 
areas; should not be a universal scheme. 
NSAP. Well-targeted. Fewer leakages reported Needs more resources. 
Delivery mechanism. A major weakness in the implementation of poverty 
alleviation programmes has been the lack of adequate participation by the people 
for whom the programmes are meant. There should be emphasis on the role of 
PRIs and NGOs. 
State Initiatives do better because of better ownership and flexibility in 
the design of programmes to suit local conditions. Examples: Gokul Gram Yojana, 
Apna Gaon Apna Kaam, Kudumshree. 
Rural Housing: Indira Awaas Yojana (1AY) became an Independent CSS 
from 1.1.1996. Free of cost houses are provided to below poverty line families. 
Unit cost is Rs.20,000 in plain and Rs.22,000 in hill/tribal areas. Updation of 
existing houses at a unit cost of Rs. 10,000 is now permissible. A new component 
of credit-cum-subsidy has also been added. In any given village/block/district 
it would take a long time before all the families are covered. This is dividing the 
poor instead of helping them to organise into groups. Despite orders, gram 
sabhas are not active in deciding beneficiaries. 
Land Reforms: Access to land is still critical for employment and income 
generation in rural areas. 
Access to land is possible through liberalisation of leasing, but leasing-in 
should be limited to small and marginal farmers. In areas characterised by feudal/ 
semi feudal modes of production, there is need to further strengthen the existing 
laws for security of tenure of the poor. 
Alienation of tribal land continues unabated but need? to be arrested. 
Gender inequality exists in both inheritance laws and land laws. Suitable 
Amendments are required to make inheritance laws to agricultural land more 
gender equal. 
342 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
There is need to update land records and to computerise them to make 
access to information easier. 
U rtoan Development, Housing and Poverty Alleviation 
Urban poverty remains an area of significant and persistent neglect in 
public policy and is a manifestation of lack of income and purchasing power 
attributable to lack of productive employment, high rate of inflation, lack of 
access to social infrastructure, affectin g the quality of life of the people. The 
1993-94 official estimate of the total urban population 'below poverty line' was 
32.36%. 
The modified urban poverty alleviation programme re-named as Swama 
Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) consists of two schemes, (a) the Urban 
Self Employment Programme (USEP) and (b) the Urban Wage Employment 
Programme (U WEP). Impact assessment has been suggested.

Technological upgradation of SSI sector 
4262. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) initiatives taken by Government to provide loan to develop technology 
for extension and development of small industries in the country before 
announcing the removal of certain restrictions on imports; 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether any fund is earmarked for the development of small, industries 
in the country; and 
(d) if so, the initial amount and the details of utilization of funds? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES, AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): (a) and (b) As per the Comprehensive Policy Package for SSI Sector 
announced on 30th August, 2000, the Government have launched a Credit 
Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation of the Small Scale 
Industries in October, 2000. The scheme provides for back ended capital subsidy 
to the extent of 12% in select products/'sub-sectors for known proven 
technologies. Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is the nodal 
agency for the Scheme being operationalized through Scheduled Commercial 
Banks/National Small Industries Corporation. An initial sum of Rs. 5 crore, as an 
advance, has been made available to SIDBI to commence the Scheme. 
(c) and (d) SIDBI has earmarked a fund of Rs. 200 crores, which has been 
subsequently enhanced by an additional Rs. KM) crores under its Technology 
Development and Modernisation Fund (TDMF) Scheme for the development of 
SSIs in the country. The cumulative sanctions and disbursement under the 
scheme since inception upto 31" March, 2001 are Rs. 462.82 crores and Rs. 
154.18 crores respectively. 
Infrastructure Development Fund 
4263. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will theMinisterof 
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to set up an Infrastructure 
Development Fund for Small Scale Industries in the country; 
359 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof: 
(c) the extent to which the industrial infrastructure of Small Scale Industries 
is expected to be upgraded: 
(d) whether the study group on policy for Small Scale Industries has 
submitted its recommendations to Government, if so. the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government for the development of Small 
Scale Industries in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES, AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
R AJE): (a) to (d) The study group on Development of Small Scale Enterprises 
was constituted by the Planning Commission in May 1999 under the Chairmanship 
of Dr. S.P. Gupta. Member, Planning Commission. The Study Group lias submitted 
its final report in March, 2001. The major recommendations include a three 
iier definition for small enterprises, a comprehensive law for the sector, including 
si mplification.of procedures, continuation of reservation, selective enhancement 
of investment limit, improving flow of credit, througli raising limit of 
composite loans, various financial and fiscal measures such as raising excise 
exemption limit and other measures and schemes for improvement of 
infrastructure, technology upgradation, marketing, etc. Recommendations inter-
alia included setting up of an Infrastructure Development Fund of the order of 
Rs. 2000 crores for Small Scale Enterprises. This fund is to be utilised to help 
the States/UTs in creating, reva mping and upgrading the industrial 
infrastructure for SMEs including upgrading the infrastructure in the existing 
industrial estates. 
(e) A number of recommendations of the Study Group have since been 
implemented through a comprehensive policy package for SSIs which will 
strengthen the Small Scale Sector and enhance its competitiveness both 
domestically and globally through easier access to credit, availability of collateral 
free composite loans upto Rs. 25 lakhs, capital subsidy for technology 
upgradation and improved infrastructure. It includes a Credit Linked Capita? 
Subsidy Scheme for Teclinology upgradation of SSIs with a provision for lending 
of Rs. 5000 crores. The other recommendations of the Study Group constitute a 
basis for the formulation of the Tenth Five Year Plan.

Achievement under Rural Employment Generation Programme 
4264. SHRI R S. GAVAI: Will theMinisterof SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES 
AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to states: 
(a) the achievements of the Rural Employment Generation Programme in 
the country, State-wise; 
(b) the provision made by Government to provide marketing and training 
facilities for the beneficiaries of such programme; and 
(c) the maimer in which Government intend to create job opportunities in 
the rural areas Uirough Khadi and Villages Industries Commission? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES. AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): (a) to (c) The Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) was 
launched on the basis of recommendations of the High Power Committee 
constituted under the then Prime Minister. This Programme is being implemented 
by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC). 
Under the REGP, the KVIC introduced a scheme namely Margin Money 
Scheme (MMS) with effect from 1.4.1995 for viable Village Industries Projects. 
The projects sanctioned under MMS as on 31.3.2000 in the country State-wise is 
as at Statement (See below). 
The Margin Money Scheme (MMS) provides 25%. of the project cost for 
the projects upto Rs. 10 lakhs as margin money grant. Forprojects above Rs. 10 
lakhs and upto Rs. 25 lakhs rate of margin money is 25% of Rs. 10 lakhs plus 10% 
of the remaining cost of the project. Special concession is being provided to SC/ 
ST/Ex-servicemen/Women/Mmority/Physically Handicapped, OBC beneficiaries 
and all the beneficiaries of North-Eastern Region, Andaman & Nicobar and 
Sikkim State wherein the margin money grant is given at the rate of 30% of the 
project cost upto Rs. 10 lakhs. 
For the development and promotion of Khadi and Village Industries, the 
Government of India announced a package for the Khadi and Village Industries 
sector on 14.05.2001. The main features of this package consist of R ebate Policy 
for five years, options of Rebate and Market Development Assistance (MD A). 
Insurance cover to Khadi artisans, emphasis on improvement of Khadi products, 
creation of packaging and design facilities, measures to promote marketing, 
brand building, cluster development, focus on core areas and provision of 
idditional working capital.

THE REGISTRATION AND OTHER RELATED LAWS 
(AMENDMENT) Bill, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY 
AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Registration Act, 
1908, the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the Indian 
Stamp Act, 1899, as passed by the Lok Sabha, be taken 
into consideration." 
Sir, this Bill has been considered, at length, by the 
Standing Committee. There are three-four different components 
of this Bill. The first is that it  has been noticed at various levels, 
both by the Central Government and the State Governments, 
that a large number of property transactions relating to transfer 
of property are being conducted by such documents wherein, 
under agreements or in part per formance of agreements, the 
possession of the property is handed over; and, across the 
country, barring a few States, the document does not require a 
registration. Because of the absence of the requirement of 
registration of those documents, it has been noticed that there is 
also a large scale evasion of stamp duty. Those documents  
become  complete  documents  because  the  possessions  are 
420 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001]  
protected. There has been a demand coming »om a large number of 
States that compulsory registration  of these documents, across the 
cduntry, be provided for, and, ther efore, this amendment seeks to 
provide for compulsory registrati on of all such agreements wherein 
part performance possession is sought to be granted. 
There was a second provision that  registration of property 
anywhere in the country could be done in the four Presidency towns. 
Some of the other States were feeling that this was leading to a loss 
of revenue, as far as those States were concerned. This was also 
leading to absence of knowledge about  those property transactions 
with the Registrars in those States, because they were registered 
elsewhere, in the four Presidency  towns. The suggestion was that 
this be done away with. 
The third suggestion was, with  which this Bill was introduced 
the fingerprint and the photograph of the person going in for the 
registration of document be there on the registered document itself. 
The Standing Committee felt that the fingerprint and the photograph 
of both, i.e., the buyer and the seller, must be on the document itself. 
The Government has accepted these suggestions. 
There is also an enabling prov ision in this Bill that all 
documents with the Registrar Office s can also be kept in computer 
floppies and disc etc., so that inspection will become easier, and 
record of those properties could be inspected throughout the country. 
Sir, the Bill found favour with the Standing Committee. This was an 
additional suggestion given by the Standing Committee which the 
Government has accepted. With thes e words, I request that this Bill 
be adopted.

Chairman, I do not have any quarrel  with the Finance Minister

incremental capital output ratio, we have to have a high rate of 
savings, to generate a high rate of investment and a high rate of

country is not doing very well, in terms of generating savings.

the East Asian countries, the sa vings of the household sector 
plus the corporate sector there is much higher than it is in our 
country. Now, if you do not want to generate savings, what is the

Government in relation to the savings, to ensure that the 
domestic savings goes up? What are the strategies and policies

more than 25 per cent of rate of saving in the country. Why is it so?

50's? Why can't the resources of t he country utilised in a meaningful

country where the foreign exchange  reserves have been high, and if 
the export is more than the import, that adds to the foreign exchange, 
and that is the way the countries build  their reserves. In our country it 
is just the other way round. Export is less than import, and we have a 
deficit. So, the ordinary rule which is followed by any country for 
building reserves, has not been followed in our country. Our foreign 
exchange reserves, if you "look at them carefully, are mainly based on 
the

concerned about fiscal deficit because the World Bank wants our 
fiscal deficit to go down. Actually , it has not gone down as was

out of control of the Government. Now the question is how to bring 
the fiscal deficit under your control. There are two ways to bridge the 
deficit, whether it is a family or an enterprise or a Government. If there 
is a deficit, you can either increase the income or decrease the 
expenditure or make a combination of the two. In our country, till now, 
I find that the alternative that y ou have adopted is not raising the 
revenue, but reducing the expenditu re, and a combination of the two.

done, but that too to a limited extent, because we cannot reduce the 
expenditure because of various reasons. Subsidy has gone up to the 
bare minimum, and the interest rates are a constitutional obligation 
that you cannot avoid. Really spea king, the reduction in expenditure 
is done within the limits. It cannot  be done beyond certain limits. Why 
don't you think more in terms of raising the revenue? This can be 
done in many ways. Once it has been proposed in the country that if 
you reduce the rate of income tax, then there will be more complaints. 
If the rate of income tax is reduce d, the income will be higher and the 
complaints will be more.  That is

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001]  
the theory. It is true that, for a year or two, this particular theory will

Why can't you have a rural wealth taxation system, which is

education, social components, etc., is reduced? You can have,

taxing the rural rich and not the rural poor. The rural rich have

removed. I have done some calculations which may or may not be 
wrong. You can raise up to Rs.27, 000 crores from this particular

feasibility study by a competent orga nisation to work out the various 
probabilities and to find out the possibilities.       But that

relate the capita! market, bank deposits and all that, has been 19.8 per 
cent in 1999-2000. This has actually gone up. But the highest ever 
was 19.7 per cent in 1994-95 when we achieved 19.8 per cent. Where 
have we taken the beating? We have taken the beating particularly in 
the public sector saving which has turned into dis-saving, that is, 1.2 
per cent. That is where I go back to the Fifth Pay Commission, and If I 
say, it was a great catastrophe that befell this nation when we decided 
to give the kind of extra which was given. It has put a burden on the 
States' finances. It has ruined the States' finances. If you look at the 
BCR of any State, you will find what had happened in 1997-98 and 
1998-99 to the Government of India's finances. It is the public sector 
dis-saving, Sir, which has been the culprit, which has declined from 
plus 2 per cent in 1995-96 to a minus 1.2. There has been some 
decline in the private corporate savings also. So, this is, as far as 
savings are concerned. In the Tenth Plan, t he Approach Paper will be 
discussed in the NDC tomorrow, in order to be able to achieve a 
growth rate of 8 per cent, the rate of investment in the economy has 
been put at 32 per cent and savings rates is expected to be pushed up 
to something like 29.8 per cent or so. We have to achieve that kind of 
savings rates during this period of fi ve years, by largely controlling our 
own fiscal deficit. 
I had an occasion in the other House, to say it clearly, and I 
would like to reiterate it here that, while the fiscal deficit is important, 
the most intractable problem has been the revenue deficit, which is 
the consumption expenditure of the Government.   Therefore, I have 
told my colleagues that 
446 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001]  
as far as investment expenditure is  concerned, whatever funds that 
are needed from the Mini stry of Finance, we will be making them 
available. But, as far as the non-Plan and, especially, the revenue 
expenditure is concerned, we sha ll keep the strictest and the most 
stringent control on that. So, the sa vings rate will have to go up and 
we will have to make sure that the public sector 'dissaving' - 'the 
minus' - is improved to 'plus' and that it goes up. 
As far as the incremental capital output ratio is concerned, 
Biplabbabu is quite right that if we  do not achieve efficiency of the 
capital employed, then, we will not be able to increase the kind of, or 
have the kind of, growth rate which we are anticipating. Therefore, 
the ICOR of 4.28 per cent, is a far cry, I agree with you, from the 3 
per cent which had been achieved earlier. But the international global 
standard - I stand corrected by the hon. Leader of the Opposition -- I 
am told, today, is around 3.9 per cent or 4 per cent. That will be 
considered to be a good ICOR and, in the Tenth Plan, what we are 
projecting to do is to bring it up to 4.08 per cent. 
About the foreign exchange reserves, I would like to say that 
there has been much talk of the vo latile nature of our reserves, the 
fact that they might run away. We know from the international 
experience that countries with much larger foreign exchange 
reserves than the $ 44.5 billion t hat we have at the moment, have 
been brought down to their knees within days because their reserves 
have gone away. But I would like to make two points here. The first 
one is: even at the height of the East  Asian crisis, even at the height 
of the sanctions, when the gloom-doom scenario was much worse 
than it is today, what was considered to be volatile, did not fly away 
from this country. It stayed. The decrease, if at all, the erosion, if at 
all, was marginal. And, since t hen, the situation has improved. 
Therefore, there is a confidence, there is a worldwide confidence, in 
India, and, I am quite sure, that conf idence will abide. And, therefore, 
the fly-by-night operators running out situation should not arise. 
The other point is, we have been extremely careful, over a 
period of time, throughout the decade of the 90s, with our short-term 
borrowings. Therefore, if you look at the foreign debt portfolio, you 
will find that the short-term borrowings are a very, very small part - 3-
4 per cent of the overall short- term borrowings that we have. 
Therefore, while we have a liberal  regime of foreign exchange 
management, there is no need to fear that the foreign exchange, 
which has accumulated o\ier a period of time, is going to go away.

THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER 
OF DEFENCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Hon. Members would recall 
that in order to create a conducive atmosphere for talks prior to the 
India-Pakistan Summit in July, 2001, the Prime Minister had 
announced certain unilateral

in   the establishment of durable peace and stability between India 
and Pakistan.

that the foundation of peace between India and Pakistan has to be 
laid in the minds and hearts of the people of both countries. 
We hold that increased trade between the two countries 
would have its own dynamics and t hat would impact positively on 
our bilateral relations. Accordingly, on 4 m July, 2001, the Prime 
Minister had instructed the Minist ry of Commerce to identify fifty 
tariff lines on which tariff could either be eliminated or reduced, on 
imports from Pakistan.

through a process of Inter-Ministerial consultations. The list is 
placed on the Table of the House.

notifications in this regard after completing all necessary procedural 
requirements. [Placed in Library.  See No. LT. 4164/01]

VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI):   The 
Monsoon Session commenced on Monday, the 23rd July, 2001, 
and we have had 29 sittings, spread over around 140 hours. 
The House sat late on few occasions beyond the normal 
working time, for more than 25 hours, to complete legislative and 
other important business. However, more than 16 hours were lost 
over four days, due to adjournments, over the working of the UTI 
and over the reported violence at the DMK rally in Chennai. 
During the Session, twelve newly elected Members 
subscribed to oath and took their seats in the House. The House 
also bade farewell to the six retiring Members from the State of 
Tamil Nadu. 
During the Session, 80 reports of various Parliamentary 
Committees were presented or laid on the Table of the House. 
During the Session, 8 new Bills were introduced; one Bill 
was withdrawn; 3 Bills were returned; and 32 Bills were passed, 
out of which, 5 Bills were fresh  Bills,   10  Bills were  Repealing  
Bills  and  17  Bills were 
452 

RAJYA SABHA [31 August, 2001]  
amending Bills, including the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) 
Bill, 2000, which extends the freeze on the number of seats in the 
Lok Sabha and the State Legislatures till 2026. The Government 
Legislative Business took 27 hours. 
There were 15 Statements in all, on (a) the summit-level 
talks held between India and Pakistan at Agra (by hon'bie Prime 
Minister); (b) incidents of killin gs in Jammu & Kashmir; (c) CNG 
supply in Delhi; (d) patent on Basmati Rice lines and grains to Rice 
Tec inc., USA; (e) setting up of Non-lapsable Special Railway 
Safety Fund for Indian Railways; and (f) promotion of Indo-
Pakistan relations; two of which were converted into full-fledged 
discussions, and, on other occasi ons, a number of clarifications 
were sought by Members spread over more than 8 hours. 
We had Calling Attention Motions on  the following  4  
subjects, which lasted for more than 14 hours: - 
(i) Rood situation in the country caused by heavy rains, 
resulting in loss of lives, property and crops; 
(ii) Recent   incidents  of  fire   in   Ordnance   Depots   in   
the country and the remedial measures taken by 
Government with regard thereto; 
(iii) Policy of disinvestment in PSUs with reference to the 
methods of valuation of their assets, the non-
transparent manner in which disinvestment is being 
done, and the remedial measures taken by 
Government with regard thereto; and 
(iv) The recent circulars of UGC and the NCERT 
curriculum framework in t he context of the National 
Policy on Education. 
We had Short Duration Discussions on the following 4 
subjects, which lasted for more than 36 hours:- 
(i) On the working of UTI with special reference to 
freeze on sale and repurchase of US-64, and failure 
of Government to take timely action; 
(ii) On   the  economic  slow  down,   fall   in   GDP   rate  
and deteriorating  financial  condition  of yhe  country  
in  the context of mid-term appraisal of the 9   Five 
Year Plan; 
(iii) On the failure of PDS and need for revamping it; and 
453 

[31 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
(iv) On the Security Scenario in the light of terrorist  and 
other internal and external security threats. 
Ten important matters, with the permission of the hon'ble 
Chairman, and two Questions of Privileges were raised by some 
Members, which lasted about one-and-half-hours. 
There were about 154 Special Mentions on Matters of 
Public Importance. 
During the Session, 580 Starred Questions and 4,430 
Unstarred Questions were admitt ed and answered. Seventy-eight 
Starred Questions were orally answered and five Statements by 
Ministers correcting Answers to Questions were made. Five notices 
for Short Notice Questions and nine notices for Half-an-Hour 
Discussions were received, but none could take place. 
During the Session, four references were made regarding 
train accident in Kerala, tragic deaths of six Amernath Yatris at 
Sheshnag, killing of some persons in Doda district and dropping of 
atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in Japan, on 6 th and 9,h 
August, 1945. 
The House also paid homage to the martyrs of the 'Quit 
India' Movement launched, under the leadership of Mahatma 
Gandhi, in 1942. 
The House paid tributes to Shaheed Udham Singh on the 
618I anniversary of his martyrdom. 
The House also condoled the deaths of King Birendra Bir 
Bikram Shah Dev and other members of the Royal family of Nepal, 
the tragic 
death of Shrimati Phoolan Devi, a sitting Member of the Lok 
Sabha, and Shri G.K. Moopnar, a sitting Memoer of this House, 
besides some other former Members. 
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Leader of 
the House, the Leader of the Oppo sition, leaders of various parties 
and groups and all the hon. Members for the kind cooperation 
extended by them in conducting the proceedings of the House. 
I do so on behalf of the Hon. Chairman, the Hon. Deputy 
Chairman, the Members on the Panel of Vice-Chairmen, and on 
my own behalf.
